extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, librarians, and stakeholders in scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: A compiled list of scholarly journals that experienced mass resignations of editors and the stated reasons for those resignations. The page catalogs incidents across disciplines and years, naming journals, publishers, and concise reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: editorial disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial disagreement — editors resigning due to disagreements over editorial direction or decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scientific Reports (2017, 'editorial disagreement'); Molecular Genetics & Genomic Medicine (2021, 'editorial disagreement'). Used when editors and publisher/owner cannot agree on editorial choices or strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: editorial interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial interference — publisher or owner intervening in editorial decisions or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: International Journal of Occupational and Environmental Health (2017, 'editorial disagreement and interference'); Diversity & Distributions (2018, 'open access fees and editorial interference'); Communications in Algebra (2026, 'running roughshod over the standard practices of the refereeing process in mathematics').

rubrics_metrics.name: open_access_policies_and_fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Open access policies and fees — disputes over OA policies, APCs, or publisher's open-access terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Journal of Informetrics (2019, 'open access policies and fees'); Journal of Biogeography (2023, 'open access policies and fees'); Journal of International Students (2023, 'transition to new management with open access fees').

rubrics_metrics.name: subscription_fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription fees — objections to changes in subscription pricing or models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lingua (2015, 'subscription fees'). Used when cost to readers/subscribers or paywall decisions prompt resignations.

rubrics_metrics.name: replacement_or_removal_of_editor_in_chief
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal/replacement/non-renewal of editors — resignations triggered by firing, replacement, or non-renewal of editor-in-chief positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Building Research and Information (2018, 'not renewing editor in chief’s contract'); Design Studies (2023, 'replacement of editor in chief'); Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics (2024, 'publisher replaced the journal’s editors without warning').

rubrics_metrics.name: pressure_to_increase_output_or_volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure to increase publication volume, output, scope, or special issues — including demands to publish more papers or expand journal scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Design Studies (2023, 'editorial interference to increase output and scope'); Journal of the Political Philosophy (2023, 'dispute over publication volume'); Journal of Geometric Mechanics (2023, 'switch to open access and editorial interference to increase output and special issues'); Journal of Clinical Immunology (2024, 'pressure to publish more papers').

rubrics_metrics.name: publisher_altering_published_content_or_issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher altered an already published issue or added material online without editorial consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Revue d’intelligence artificielle (2019, after the new publisher 'altered an already published issue' and 'a special issue had been added online'); Ingénierie des Systèmes d’Information (2019, 'several issues...published without our supervision').

rubrics_metrics.name: predatory_publishing_practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of predatory publishing practices by the publisher/company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Publications (MDPI, 2023, company's 'predatory publishing practices'). Used when editors cite business practices that prioritize revenue over quality/ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: no_reject_or_fundamental_editorial_model_change
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental change in editorial model (e.g., instituting a 'no-reject' policy) or other major policy shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: eLife (2023, institution of 'no-reject' publishing model and firing of editor in chief). Such model changes that alter peer review/selection criteria can prompt resignations.

rubrics_metrics.name: takeover_or_change_of_publisher_management
rubrics_metrics.description: Takeover/acquisition or transition to new management/publisher that changes journal governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kurdish Studies (2023, takeover by Intellectual Edge Research Publishing); Amsterdam University Press (2025, after Taylor & Francis acquired majority of its English-language book program); Journal of International Students (2023, 'transition to new management').

rubrics_metrics.name: contract_or_terms_changes_between_society_and_publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractual changes or renegotiated terms between a society that owns a journal and the publisher that affect journal governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Indoor Air (2022, society terminated agreement due to changes in terms); Sedimentology (2025, contract changes between Wiley and the society).

rubrics_metrics.name: workload_and_compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive workload or inadequate compensation for editors leading to resignations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aging Cell (2022, 'workload and compensation').

rubrics_metrics.name: treatment_and_pressure_on_reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure on, or poor treatment of, reviewers (including demands that may undermine review quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sustainable Organisations section of Frontiers in Sustainability (2023, 'pressure on and treatment of reviewers' and related resignation letter of 31 editors).

rubrics_metrics.name: publisher_staffing_or_operational_changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational changes such as office closures, layoffs, or moving operations that affect editorial functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Journal of Molecular Medicine (2018, 'office closure with layoffs and new editor in chief'); GigaScience (2025, 'firing the editors and moving the journal’s operations').

rubrics_metrics.name: lack_of_editorial_input_on_appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of input by editors on appointments to editorial boards or editor-in-chief selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Journal of Clinical Immunology (2024, 'lack of input on editorial board members'); Intelligence (2024, editor in chief appointments 'ignored suggestions made by the long-time editor').

rubrics_metrics.name: failure_to_handle_allegations_or_ethics_issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher/journal failing to properly handle allegations (e.g., misconduct, problematic papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth (2024, 'objections to journal’s failure to handle allegations'); British Journal of Psychiatry (2023, resignations following owner's decision not to retract controversial paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: ideology_or_censorship_driven_actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher or owner actions perceived as ideological censorship or targeting of particular views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gender, Work and Organization (2024, protest of an 'anti-woke' drive against radical views in the pursuit of profits).

rubrics_metrics.name: cancellation_of_planned_editorial_content
rubrics_metrics.description: Cancellation of planned special issues or theme issues by the parent association or publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Journal of Architectural Education (2025, after the parent association cancelled an upcoming theme issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: over_expansion_and_price_increases_harming_quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher multiplying number of publications while increasing prices, allegedly at the expense of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Revue des Composites et des Matériaux Avancés (2026, claiming publisher 'multiplied the number of publications while increasing prices at the expense of quality').

rubrics_metrics.name: undermining_peer_review_standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions that 'run roughshod' over standard practices of refereeing or otherwise undermine peer review integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Communications in Algebra (2026, 'running roughshod over the standard practices of the refereeing process in mathematics').

rubrics_metrics.name: series_of_concerning_decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of publisher or management decisions judged by editors as 'deeply concerning' and potentially detrimental to the journal's future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Journal of Approximation Theory (2026, resignations for 'a series of decisions that a substantial majority of the editors found deeply concerning and potentially detrimental to the journal’s future'). This is a catch-all for cumulative harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: desire_to_create_more_accessible_publication_models
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors resigning to found or move to a more accessible publishing model (e.g., Diamond Open Access) as a positive raison d'être.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Journal of Philosophical Logic (2025, editors launching a new Diamond Open Access journal 'to make academic research ... as accessible as possible').

rubrics_metrics.name: concerns_about_review_times_and_editorial_process_efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns arising from review times or editorial process inefficiencies used as reasons for mass resignations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Criminology (2025, 'after an analysis of review times at the journal' and 'an unworkable relationship with the current Executive Board').
